title: Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control

author: Katherine C. Kellogg · Melissa A. Valentine · Angèle Christin

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied material is only fragmented bibliography text. Although the cited topics—algorithmic management, worker quantification and people analytics—are broadly relevant to organisational power, they do not reveal the source authors’ own position on whether AI redistributes legal tasks, status or professional exclusivity.
qs: with machines: The impact of algorithmic and data-      driven management on human workers.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s work-redesign thesis by finding that algorithms create and reconfigure work and require substantial human implementation and maintenance. It materially extends the proposition with a worker-centered labor-process account: deployment choices also redistribute managerial control, autonomy and voice, so operating-model redesign should include worker participation, training and safeguards against opaque or unappealable control.
qs: But existing studies consistently show that employers’ use of algorithms can also create or reconfigure forms of work (e.g., Anteby, Chan, & DiBenigno, 2016; Autor, 2015a, 2015b; Davenport & Kirby, 2016).

st.t: Worker power: Automation outcomes depend on consultation
st.an: The source accepts the contingent account that workplace outcomes reflect organisational design and worker power rather than technology alone. It materially develops the proposition through a labour-process analysis of algorithmic control, evidence of contrasting managerial practices, and a research agenda on worker voice, training, transparency and collective governance, while treating consultation benefits as promising rather than guaranteed.
qs: Because these studies demonstrate that neither the technologies themselves nor the type of work dictates the ways that employers use algorithmic control systems, what factors do shape this?

kp.k: Interdisciplinary review supplies a workplace-control framework
kp.d: This article, published online on 21 November 2019 and in Academy of Management Annals 14(1) in 2020, synthesizes research across occupations and industries rather than offering a legal-services-specific forecast. Its methods describe reviewing more than 1,100 articles reporting empirical studies of algorithmic, crowd, or platform technologies, using 2005 as a loose starting point. The authors also included case studies and practitioner publications as motivating examples where developments outpaced peer-reviewed research.
qs: We based our analysis on a review of more than 1,100 articles that reported an empirical study of algorithmic, crowd, or platform technologies.
We selected 2005 as the loose starting point, a period that represented an inflection point in algorithmic capabilities.

kp.k: Algorithms are contested instruments, not merely efficiency tools
kp.d: Drawing on Edwards’ labor-process framework, the authors argue that employers use technologies to capture value from labor while workers resist to preserve autonomy, dignity, and identity. They acknowledge evidence of improved decision-making, coordination, and organizational learning, but challenge research that treats economic benefits as the principal outcome. Their account of algorithms embodying powerful actors’ interests is a theoretical interpretation of the reviewed evidence, not a claim that all implementations produce identical effects.
qs: What they miss is an understanding of algorithmic systems as instruments of control that are contested between employers and workers.

It allows us to understand algorithmic systems not as neutral tools that facilitate efficiency and improve communication exchanges, but as contested instruments of control that carry specific ideological preferences (Winner, 1980).

kp.k: Six mechanisms organize algorithmic workplace control
kp.d: The central synthesis distinguishes direction through restricting and recommending, evaluation through recording and rating, and discipline through replacing and rewarding. Direction specifies tasks, sequencing, timing, and accuracy; evaluation reviews performance; discipline uses punishment and rewards to secure compliance. These categories describe organizational control, not model benchmarking or human checking of AI-generated legal work.
qs: We find that algorithmic control in the workplace operates through six main mechanisms, which we call the “6 Rs”—employers can use algorithms to direct workers by restricting and recommending, evaluate workers by recording and rating, and discipline workers by replacing and rewarding.

kp.k: Algorithmic control differs from earlier rational control
kp.d: The authors distinguish technical control embedded in production technologies from bureaucratic control embodied in standardized rules and roles. Algorithmic technologies can extend both through comprehensive data collection, instantaneous feedback, interactive participation, and opacity. They qualify these distinctions as ideal types that can coexist in hybrid systems, rather than a universal historical replacement of one regime by another.
qs: Specifically, we describe how algorithmic technologies can be more comprehensive, instantaneous, interactive, and opaque than prior workplace technologies (Table 1).
These different systems of rational control should be viewed as ideal types; in practice, models of control frequently overlap and can be combined in hybrid forms

kp.k: Recommendations improve decisions while redirecting professional judgment
kp.d: Algorithmic recommending steers workers toward choices preferred by the system’s designers, sometimes bypassing professional heuristics. As a beneficial example, the review reports Gupta’s account of Crisis Text Line: identifying “ibuprofen” as 16 times more likely than “suicide” to predict emergency aid helped reduce response time for high-risk texters from 120 seconds to 39 seconds. Other reviewed studies describe opaque recommendations frustrating salespeople, increasing diagnostic ambiguity for healthcare professionals, and provoking resentment among judges and prosecutors.
qs: Algorithmic recommending entails employers using algorithms to offer suggestions intended to prompt the targeted worker to make decisions preferred by the choice architect.
Their algorithmic system identified that the term “ibuprofen” was 16 times more likely to predict the need for emergency aid than the word “suicide.”
Similarly, Christin (2017) shows that judges and prosecutors resented the opacity of predictive algorithms called riskassessment tools because they found them to be unintelligible.

kp.k: Algorithmic bias can reproduce unequal patterns of scrutiny
kp.d: The review identifies historical discrimination and unrepresentative samples as two routes through which training data can generate discriminatory recommendations. It reports research on criminal-risk assessment and predictive policing, including the possibility that directing enforcement toward already scrutinized groups generates additional observations about those groups. Crucially, the authors state that missing counterfactuals prevent a general conclusion that algorithmic processes are better or worse than their predecessors.
qs: In the current literature, the lack of counterfactuals means that it is not clear if and when these new processes are worse or better than the older processes.
First, historical data can reflect existing patterns of inequality and discrimination.
Second, algorithms can draw inferences from a biased sample of the population.

kp.k: Restrictions narrow choices, communication, and worker voice
kp.d: Algorithmic restricting controls which information workers see and which actions they can take, potentially instantaneously and covertly. Examples include narrowing delivery and shift choices, restricting pharmacy assistants’ robot-loading requests, and Upwork chatbot warnings against off-platform communication. Restrictive interfaces and anonymized identifiers can also prevent workers from contacting requesters, managers, or one another, reducing their ability to challenge decisions or identify abusive clients.
qs: It entails the use of algorithms to display only certain information and allow specific behaviors while preventing others.
However, algorithmic restricting can limit worker voice more extensively than before.
These restrictions often prevented workers from ever speaking directly with a human manager

kp.k: Task fragmentation can intensify labor-market precarity
kp.d: The review links platform work to discrete or micro-task allocation, unpredictable scheduling, and information asymmetries. It reports examples including food-delivery workers choosing only among algorithmically displayed shifts and orders, Upwork profiles becoming private after 30 days without work, and Mechanical Turk requesters rating workers without reciprocal requester ratings. These are historically situated examples from the reviewed literature, not assertions about platforms’ current policies.
qs: Second, jobs are frequently broken down into discrete or even “micro” tasks, which can be scheduled in finely grained, opaque, and unpredictable ways.
Workers on the Upwork platform who did not work for 30 days had their profile status changed to private so that clients could not find them (Jarrahi et al., 2019).

kp.k: Recording expands surveillance beyond conventional productivity measurement
kp.d: Algorithmic recording aggregates detailed internal and external data, often in real time, to evaluate behavior and output. Reviewed examples include employee communications, sentiments, task duration, driving behavior, and wearable-device data extending beyond working hours. The authors identify privacy loss, self-policing, inaccurate data, and difficulty correcting records as potential consequences, particularly when workers do not know what information is collected.
qs: Algorithmic recording entails the use of computational procedures to monitor, aggregate, and report, often in real time, a wide range of finely grained data from internal and external sources.
This surveillance can extend control beyond work hours, as some employers have given workers wearable devices that rewarded lifestyle choices such as exercise and sleep (O’Connor, 2015).
Because workers may not be aware of the data being collected about their behavior and performance, they may not be able to appeal judgments against them or correct missing or mistaken information.

kp.k: Ratings govern reputation, hiring, and future opportunities
kp.d: Algorithmic rating combines internal and external assessments and can predict future performance, expertise, up-skilling needs, or turnover intentions. The review describes ratings becoming public reputational assets that govern access to projects and visibility, with small, volatile, or erroneous changes potentially excluding workers. Customer-generated ratings introduce discrimination risks and less accountability than an ongoing managerial relationship; the authors present their legal treatment as uncertain.
qs: Managers are now often using computational technologies to gather ratings and rankings to calculate some measure of workers’ performance, as well as predictive analytics to predict measures of their future performance.
Consequently, algorithmic ratings have become an essential reputational asset for workers.
Workers also have fewer mechanisms for contesting unfair evaluations (Rosenblat et al., 2017; Rosenblat & Stark, 2016).

kp.k: Replacing disciplines workers through rapid substitution
kp.d: The authors explicitly distinguish workplace-level algorithmic replacing from macroeconomic replacement of jobs by automation. Here, algorithms remove or deactivate workers and facilitate hiring substitutes, sometimes automatically when ratings fall below thresholds. Global recruitment and automated screening can increase insecurity, especially for less-skilled workers, while the review also reports that specialized workers may gain opportunities and recruiting platforms may improve access to underrepresented candidates.
qs: Algorithmic replacing entails rapidly or even automatically firing underperforming workers from the organization and replacing them with substitute workers.
we examine algorithmic replacement at the workplace level with a focus on how itcanbeusedbyemployersasamechanismofcontrol.
workers with specialized skills may gain even more opportunities, whereas workers with fewer skills become even more powerless.

kp.k: Dynamic rewards and gamification can intensify effort
kp.d: Algorithmic rewarding allocates pay, work, flexibility, or advancement dynamically in response to behavior. The authors describe gamification as potentially making work enjoyable while also manufacturing consent, encouraging unpaid contributions, and weakening workers’ ability to set limits. Citing Lehdonvirta (2018), they report Mechanical Turk tasks generally yielding $1–2/hour on average, with occasional tasks offering $10–$20/hour, prompting workers to gamble time on better opportunities. Opaque reward rules and rapid pay changes can create frustration and stress.
qs: It entails using algorithms to interactively and dynamically reward high-performing workers with more opportunities, higher pay, and promotions.
Gamification can also be used to encourage unremunerated work by both external and internal workers (Edery & Mollick, 2009).
Workers could thus gamble with their time, foregoing modest but certain rewards for a chance to earn bigger rewards (Lehdonvirta, 2018).

kp.k: Opacity can conceal managerial choices and value distribution
kp.d: The review distinguishes opacity arising from intentional secrecy, limited technical literacy, and machine-learning complexity. Through a labor-process interpretation, the authors argue that employers can deliberately create information asymmetries that constrain choices and obscure how gains are distributed. Narratives of fully automated systems may conceal employer intervention in architecture, nudges, and sanctions, making targets for worker contestation harder to identify.
qs: Last, algorithms can be opaque, for three main reasons: intentional secrecy, required technical literacy, and machine-learning opacity (Burrell, 2016).
The opaque nature of algorithmic control can allow employers to track what workers are doing but limit workers’ understanding of employers’ strategies.

kp.k: Managerial disintermediation reduces opportunities for appeal
kp.d: Beyond the four technological affordances, the authors identify removal of human managerial intermediaries as a distinct feature of algorithmic control. Full automation can eliminate discretionary exceptions, explanations, assistance, and opportunities to appeal to human empathy. They raise accountability and procedural fairness as research questions rather than demonstrating that every automated system lacks recourse.
qs: algorithmic systems enable the disintermediation of managers around the direction, evaluation, and disciplining of workers.

When managerial decisions are fully automated, there are fewer opportunities for workers to appeal to the empathy of human decision-makers, and often fewer rule exceptions granted (Aneesh, 2009; Lee et al., 2015; Schildt, 2017).
Who is accountable and responsible when things go wrong, and what are some potential mechanisms for holding actors accountable?

kp.k: Work design mediates benefits and harms
kp.d: The review rejects technological determinism: worker outcomes vary across organizations, individuals, skills, and countries. Reported mitigating practices include supportive managerial relationships, predictable dispute resolution, paid coordination and training tasks, and channels for collaboration. CloudFactory’s more orderly task allocation is contrasted with Mechanical Turk’s competitive marketplace; some Uber drivers perceived autonomy, and some platform workers valued flexibility and task variety. Worker voice, training, and education partnerships are proposed as areas for further research and implementation inquiry.
qs: Organizations can facilitate more positive outcomes for workers both through informal managerial practices and through formal structuring of the work process.
Because these studies demonstrate that neither the technologies themselves nor the type of work dictates the ways that employers use algorithmic control systems, what factors do shape this?
Team leaders and junior managers were paid for the time that they spent checking the quality of crowd-workers’ tasks and answeringcrowd-workers’questions(Gray&Suri,2019).

kp.k: Automation creates curation, brokerage, and articulation work
kp.d: The authors identify three emerging forms of occupational work alongside task elimination. Curation prepares and interprets data, often through outsourced and poorly visible contingent labor; brokerage translates and promotes algorithmic outputs across occupational groups; articulation coordinates interdependencies and repairs failures. Such work supports employer control but can also give workers discretion, new jurisdictions, and opportunities to resist. The review does not quantify the net employment balance.
qs: But existing studies consistently show that employers’ use of algorithms can also create or reconfigure forms of work
they require considerable work to develop, fine-tune, implement, maintain, and change over time
algorithmic curation, algorithmic brokerage, and algorithmic articulation.

kp.k: Human interpretation and repair remain essential
kp.d: The review contrasts rhetoric of fully automated AI with continuing human dependence. Police intelligence officers intended to implement predictive outputs instead exercised subjective interpretation; micro-workers resolved Uber identity checks that algorithms could not confidently match after appearance changes. These examples show that implementation and failure handling create human work and discretion rather than simply removing human participation.
qs: human curation remains essential to make most algorithmic technologies function correctly
the intelligence officers began to steer police action based on their own—largely subjective—interpretations.

Thus, a new form of articulation work involves handling the unpredictable failures of algorithmic technology interdependence by applying flexibility, situational adaptability, creativity, interpersonal interaction, or persuasion.

kp.k: Emerging occupations create training and professionalization questions
kp.d: The authors call for research into the skills, career paths, and professionalization of algorithmic occupations, including how brokers explain opaque systems and how lower-power experts influence others. They report—not validate—a McKinsey Global Institute forecast that US demand for algorithmic “translators” would reach two to four million by 2026. Their discussion includes computational-thinking education, on-the-job training, coding boot camps, and coordinated pathways across secondary and postsecondary education.
qs: A report by McKinsey Global Institute estimates that, by 2026, in the United States alone, the demand for algorithmic “translators” will reach two to four million.
More research is needed to understand the structure, professionalization, and career paths of these emerging occupations.

kp.k: Individual resistance includes professional noncooperation and gaming
kp.d: The authors identify noncooperation, leveraging algorithms, and personal negotiation with clients as individual resistance strategies. Reviewed legal-professional examples include ignoring risk scores, manipulating inputs to obtain desired scores, criticizing data and methods, and obstructing data collection. Other workers reverse-engineered ratings, used scripts to identify work, or negotiated client ratings. Some contractors worked for free to protect reputations, showing that resistance could carry costs and contribute to ratings inflation.
qs: We find three main individual practical strategies of resistance: noncooperation, leveraging algorithms, and personal negotiation with clients.

Christin (2017) demonstrates that web journalists and legal professionals engaged in foot-dragging (ignoring risk scores and analytics systems in their daily work), gaming (manipulating the variables they entered in algorithmic systems to obtain the score that they desired)
when problems arose, the contractors often offered to work for free in exchange for good ratings (Rahman, 2017).

kp.k: Collective organizing can counter platform information asymmetries
kp.d: Under the label “algoactivism,” the review describes online forums, worker-created rating systems, strikes, reverse surveillance, and platform cooperatives. Turkopticon enables workers to evaluate requesters; Dynamo supports collective mobilization. Cooperatives and peer-production communities illustrate governance alternatives in which control can reflect shared member values. The authors retain uncertainty about effectiveness, including whether reverse surveillance can restore power when employers retain proprietary algorithms and larger datasets.
qs: Instead, they have begun to organize using online forums and platforms and through platform cooperativism.
Such forums and platforms can help workers address the lack of voice and information asymmetries that are often associated with algorithmic control in a variety of ways.
it is an open question whether sousveillance can restore workers’ power because employees do not usually have access to the employers’ large data sets and proprietary algorithms (Danaher, 2016).

kp.k: Public critique and documentation support algorithmic accountability
kp.d: The review describes fairness, accountability, and transparency discourse as another form of resistance. It reports how ProPublica’s 2016 analysis of more than 10,000 criminal defendant files in Broward County prompted competing interpretations of COMPAS fairness and broader stakeholder discussion. It also reports professional ethics initiatives and advocates’ proposals for short model cards documenting intended uses, performance, bias, limitations, and recommendations; these are governance proposals, not demonstrated universal remedies.
qs: The different parties offered distinct measurements of algorithmic fairness and conflicting justifications for using them (Feller, Pierson, Corbett-Davies, & Goel, 2016).

These activists argued in favor of providing “model cards,” short (one to two page) documents for trained machine-learning models that would include core metrics about bias, fairness, and inclusion (Gebru et al., 2017; Mitchell et al., 2019).

kp.k: Legal mobilization contests surveillance and employment classification
kp.d: The authors describe worker efforts involving privacy, discrimination, surveillance, and contractor classification. Reported examples include UPS union restrictions on undisclosed tracking and discipline based solely on data, litigation against platforms, GDPR impact-assessment requirements, and California’s 2019 AB 5 following Dynamex. The article presents implementation and consequences as unsettled at publication, asking how these frameworks would reshape platform work rather than claiming subsequent outcomes.
qs: First, workers and labor organizers have advocated for workplace and legal policies to protect employee privacy, limit managerial surveillance, prevent discrimination, and reclassify independent contractors as employees.

Legislative efforts took place in California following the Dynamex decision and the California Assembly Bill 5 (AB 5), which in 2019 restricted the use of independent contractors by imposing the so-called ABC test.

kp.k: Worker data ownership remains a contested policy proposal
kp.d: The review reports advocates’ proposals to treat data as compensated labor and to let individuals rent or sell data through collective intermediaries. It distinguishes the value of worker data from their use for managerial control. The authors propose research into whether ownership arrangements improve worker outcomes or instead produce unequal privacy protection, with affluent workers able to retain data and low-income workers pressured to sell.
qs: Activists have argued in favor of giving people ownership of their digital data and in favor of treating data as a form of labor that needs to be compensated
allowing a twotiered landscape where affluent workers can hold on to their personal data and protect their privacy, whereas low-income workers cannot?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin argue that algorithmic technologies reshape workplace control, create and reconfigure occupations, and provoke worker resistance.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain review of workplace algorithms, including machine learning, rather than a prediction about generative AI or legal-service markets. The authors identify six mechanisms: recommending and restricting direct work; recording and rating evaluate workers; replacing and rewarding discipline them. They argue that algorithmic control can expand surveillance, personalize interventions, restrict information and opportunities, and reduce access to human managers. Crucially, 'replacing' principally means using algorithms to dismiss workers and recruit substitute workers, not replacing human labor with AI. Separately, they argue that automation can eliminate tasks while creating curation, brokerage, and articulation work needed to develop, interpret, integrate, maintain, and repair systems. Their synthesis also identifies individual resistance, platform organizing, public fairness advocacy, and legal mobilization. Legal-sector examples concern criminal-justice professionals resisting predictive tools and discriminatory risks in criminal-justice decisions, not law-firm staffing, billing, or legal-AI vendor competition.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims derive from an interdisciplinary literature review organized through labor process theory, with empirical studies and practitioner examples rather than a new experiment or model benchmark.
pts.d: The methods appendix reports reviewing more than 1,100 articles about algorithmic, crowd, or platform technologies. Searches covered Web of Science and Google Scholar, followed by screening for empirical work contexts, citation searches, practitioner and case-study supplementation, and expert consultation. The underlying evidence includes observations, archival or trace data, and surveys. The six-mechanism framework is the authors' synthesis using Edwards' direction–evaluation–discipline typology. Examples include platform-worker monitoring and deactivation, warehouse performance tracking, differences between microwork platforms, and human work repairing algorithmic failures. For criminal justice, the authors draw on Christin (2017) for professional resistance and Angwin et al. (2016), alongside Corbett-Davies et al. (2017), for risk-assessment disparities and competing fairness considerations. These are cited findings, not new measurements conducted in this review. The authors also report a McKinsey Global Institute forecast of demand for algorithmic translators; that numerical forecast belongs to the cited report, not to an independently estimated projection by the review authors.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims describe developments documented by the article's 2019 publication, with effects conditional on organizational design, worker characteristics, and implementation.
pts.d: Published online in November 2019 and in the 2020 journal volume, the review uses 2005 as a loose starting point for its empirical search. Its main claims describe existing or emerging practices rather than predicting a dated transition to autonomous workplaces. The authors describe technological affordances as possibilities, not inevitable outcomes: algorithms can be more comprehensive, instantaneous, interactive, and opaque. They expressly recognize variation across organizations and individuals, including managerial support and work structures that can improve experiences. Specialized workers may gain opportunities while less-skilled workers face greater insecurity. They acknowledge that missing counterfactuals limit comparisons between algorithmic discrimination and earlier processes. The 2026 translator-demand estimate is a separately attributed forecast. Questions about the future effects of regulation, worker data ownership, cooperative platforms, and managerial disintermediation are research questions rather than established predictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups include employers, managers, employees, platform contractors, emerging algorithmic occupations, and members of the public subject to algorithmically informed decisions.
pts.d: Employers can gain coordination efficiencies and tighter control over work, performance, compensation, and hiring. Workers can experience privacy loss, reduced autonomy and voice, discriminatory ratings, precarious access to work, and stress, although some experience greater flexibility and opportunity. Managers may be bypassed by automated decisions, reducing workers' access to discretionary exceptions and appeals. Data curators, translators or brokers, engineers, consultants, and other integration workers perform work necessary to make algorithmic systems operate; these roles can also provide new opportunities for occupational influence. In criminal justice, the review describes legal professionals resisting risk scores and data collection, while defendants and heavily monitored communities can be affected by biased predictions and enforcement feedback loops. Worker advocates, unions, and regulators contest surveillance, discrimination, employment classification, and data ownership. The source does not establish effects on legal-service prices, law-firm leverage, associate hiring, or access to civil legal assistance.
